person.name: Albert_Einstein
person.summary: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist whose work fundamentally reshaped modern physics. Working at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern, he published his 1905 ‘annus mirabilis’ papers, introducing special relativity, explaining the photoelectric effect, and providing strong evidence for atoms. In 1915 he completed general relativity, a geometric theory of gravitation that transformed our understanding of space, time, and cosmology. He received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his explanation of the photoelectric effect, later emigrated from Nazi Germany to the United States, and spent his final decades at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where he worked on unified field theories and spoke out on pacifism, Zionism, and nuclear weapons.

events.title: Birth in Ulm
events.description: Albert Einstein was born on 14 March 1879 in Ulm, then part of the Kingdom of Württemberg in the German Empire, to Hermann Einstein and Pauline Koch, secular Ashkenazi Jews. He was the couple’s first child, arriving just before the family moved east to the larger commercial centre of Munich. Though he would spend only his first year in Ulm, Einstein later cited his Swabian origins and early family background in small-scale engineering and trade as formative influences. His father and uncle were already experimenting with the rapidly developing field of electrical technology, foreshadowing Einstein’s lifelong engagement with physics and electricity.

events.title: Family moves to Munich
events.description: In 1880 the Einstein family left Ulm for Munich’s borough of Ludwigsvorstadt-Isarvorstadt, where Hermann Einstein and his brother Jakob founded Elektrotechnische Fabrik J. Einstein & Cie, a small firm producing direct‑current electrical equipment. The move placed Albert in a more industrial, urban environment during his formative years and exposed him early to technical discussions and factory life. He attended St. Peter’s Catholic elementary school and later the Luitpold Gymnasium, where he received a demanding classical and scientific education but chafed under its rote learning and strict discipline. These early experiences helped shape both his strong mathematical ability and his lifelong suspicion of authoritarian educational methods.

events.date_note: Einstein passed his Matura in September 1896 and enrolled at the Swiss Federal Polytechnic (later ETH Zürich) the following month
events.title: Passes Matura and enrolls at Zürich Polytechnic
events.description: After leaving the Luitpold Gymnasium and joining his family in Italy, Albert Einstein completed his secondary schooling at the cantonal school in Aarau, Switzerland. There he thrived in a more liberal intellectual climate and in September 1896 passed his Matura examinations with top grades in subjects such as physics and mathematics. In January 1896 he had already renounced his Württemberg citizenship to avoid conscription into the German army, effectively becoming stateless. In October 1896 he entered the mathematics and physics teaching diploma programme at the Swiss Federal Polytechnic School in Zürich, laying the formal groundwork for his later career as a theoretical physicist.

images.caption: Certificate of maturity issued to Albert Einstein in 1896 after his successful completion of secondary schooling in Aarau, Switzerland.

events.date_note: Einstein began work at the Swiss Patent Office in 1902; his four ‘annus mirabilis’ papers and his doctoral thesis appeared in 1905
events.title: Patent Office work and annus mirabilis
events.description: In 1902 Albert Einstein obtained a position as a technical expert, third class, at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern, examining applications for electromagnetic devices. The routine but intellectually stimulating work left him time for independent research, and in 1905 he submitted his doctoral dissertation to the University of Zurich and published four epoch‑making papers in Annalen der Physik. These works explained the photoelectric effect, provided a quantitative theory of Brownian motion, introduced special relativity with its new kinematics of space and time, and derived the mass–energy equivalence formula E = mc². Together they transformed Einstein from an obscure patent clerk into one of the leading theoretical physicists of his generation.

images.caption: Cover page of Albert Einstein’s 1905 doctoral dissertation submitted to the University of Zurich.

events.date_note: Einstein and Mileva Marić married in January 1903; their sons Hans Albert and Eduard were born in 1904 and 1910, respectively
events.title: Marriage to Mileva Marić and young family
events.description: In January 1903 Albert Einstein married Mileva Marić, a Serbian physicist and former fellow student from Zürich Polytechnic, in a civil ceremony in Bern. The couple had already had a daughter, Lieserl, born secretly in Serbia around early 1902, whose fate remains uncertain; she either died in infancy or was given up for adoption. In 1904 their son Hans Albert was born in Bern, followed by a second son, Eduard, in Zurich in July 1910. During these years the Einsteins moved as Albert shifted from patent‑office work to university positions, but the marriage became increasingly strained, especially as his scientific fame grew and his emotional life became entangled with his cousin Elsa Löwenthal. The relationship deteriorated into permanent separation after 1914 and ended in divorce in 1919.

images.caption: Albert Einstein with his first wife, Mileva Marić, with whom he shared both family life and early scientific discussions.

events.date_note: Einstein moved to Berlin in April 1914 to join the Prussian Academy of Sciences; in 1917 he became director of the newly founded Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics
events.title: Moves to Berlin and joins Prussian Academy
events.description: In April 1914 Einstein moved from Zurich to Berlin after accepting a prestigious appointment to the Prussian Academy of Sciences and a professorship at the Humboldt University of Berlin. The position, arranged in part by Max Planck, freed him from most teaching duties and gave him unparalleled time for research at the centre of German science. The relocation, however, deepened tensions with his wife Mileva, who disliked Berlin and soon returned to Zurich with their sons. In 1917 Einstein became the founding director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics, cementing his leadership role in German theoretical physics on the eve of his most important work on gravitation.

events.date_note: On 25 November 1915 Einstein presented to the Prussian Academy the field equations of general relativity in their final form
events.title: Presents general theory of relativity
events.description: On 25 November 1915, after several intense weeks of revising his ideas, Albert Einstein presented to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin the final form of his field equations for the general theory of relativity. This theory extended special relativity to include gravitation by describing gravity not as a force but as the curvature of spacetime produced by mass and energy. Over the following year he explored cosmological and astrophysical consequences, including models of the universe as a whole. General relativity fundamentally altered the conceptual foundations of physics and would soon be tested by astronomical observations.

events.date_note: Two eclipse expeditions, led from Principe (West Africa) and Sobral (Brazil), observed the 29 May 1919 total solar eclipse
events.title: Solar eclipse confirms relativity
events.description: On 29 May 1919, during a total solar eclipse, British expeditions led by Arthur Eddington to the island of Príncipe and to Sobral, Brazil, photographed background stars whose apparent positions would reveal whether starlight was bent by the Sun’s gravity as predicted by Einstein’s general relativity. Analysis of the plates showed a deflection consistent with Einstein’s theory and incompatible with Newtonian gravity. When the results were publicly announced later that year, they catapulted Einstein to global fame and framed general relativity as a revolutionary new understanding of space, time, and gravitation.

images.caption: One of the eclipse plates from Sobral, Brazil, used in 1919 to test Einstein’s prediction that starlight would be deflected by the Sun’s gravity.

events.date_note: Einstein sailed for the United States in April 1921 with Chaim Weizmann on the SS Rotterdam for a fund‑raising and lecture tour
events.title: First voyage to America with Weizmann
events.description: In April 1921 Einstein embarked from Europe on the SS Rotterdam with Zionist leader Chaim Weizmann for his first visit to the United States. The trip combined scientific lectures—where he expounded his relativity theories to American audiences—with an intensive fund‑raising campaign for the planned Hebrew University of Jerusalem. The journey marked Einstein’s emergence as a global public figure whose opinions on politics, Zionism, and pacifism were increasingly sought alongside his scientific ideas. It also began a lasting association with Jewish cultural and educational projects in Palestine.

images.caption: Chaim Weizmann, his wife, and Albert Einstein aboard the SS Rotterdam en route to the United States in April 1921.

events.date_note: Einstein was awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics and delivered his Nobel lecture in 1923 after returning from Japan
events.title: Awarded Nobel Prize in Physics
events.description: On 10 December 1922 Albert Einstein was formally awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics in Stockholm. The prize citation honoured “his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect”, recognising his 1905 work that had helped launch quantum theory. Because he was travelling in Asia, Einstein did not attend the main ceremony, but later delivered his Nobel lecture on relativity in Gothenburg in 1923. The award cemented his status not just as a revolutionary theorist but as a central figure in the international scientific community.

events.title: Joins League of Nations intellectual committee
events.description: In 1922 Einstein accepted appointment to the International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation of the League of Nations, based in Geneva. The committee, a forerunner of UNESCO, sought to foster scientific and cultural exchanges across national borders in the wake of World War I. Although often frustrated by bureaucracy and by nationalist politics, Einstein used the position to advocate internationalism, academic freedom, and reconciliation between former enemy nations. His participation underlined his belief that scientists bore a special responsibility to work for peace and cross‑cultural understanding.

images.caption: Plenary session of the League of Nations’ International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation in the Palais Wilson, Geneva, mid‑1920s.

events.date_note: Einstein’s British landing card records his arrival at Dover from Ostend on 26 May 1933, part of his decision not to return to Nazi Germany
events.title: Breaks with Nazi Germany and resettles abroad
events.description: After Adolf Hitler’s rise to power in January 1933, Einstein—then on a lecture tour in the United States—resolved not to return to Germany. He resigned from the Prussian Academy, denounced Nazi antisemitism, and had his property in Germany confiscated. On 26 May 1933 he arrived at Dover from Ostend, as recorded on his British landing card, en route to a temporary academic refuge in Oxford and other European and American institutions. Later that year he accepted a permanent position at the newly founded Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, marking a decisive shift of his life and work to the United States.

images.caption: Einstein’s 26 May 1933 British landing card, recording his arrival at Dover from Ostend and his onward journey to Oxford after breaking with Nazi Germany.

events.title: Signs Einstein–Szilard letter on atomic bombs
events.description: On 2 August 1939 Albert Einstein signed a letter drafted by Hungarian physicist Leó Szilárd, addressed to U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, warning that recent advances in nuclear fission might enable Nazi Germany to build extremely powerful atomic bombs. Written at Einstein’s summer retreat on Long Island, the letter urged the United States to begin its own research programme and to secure uranium supplies. Delivered to Roosevelt in October 1939, the Einstein–Szilard letter helped spur the chain of events that led to the creation of the Advisory Committee on Uranium and eventually the Manhattan Project. Einstein himself was not involved in weapons work but later expressed regret that his warning had contributed indirectly to the nuclear arms race.

images.caption: Scan of the 2 August 1939 letter to U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, drafted by Leó Szilárd and signed by Albert Einstein, warning of the possibility of German atomic bombs.

events.title: Becomes a United States citizen
events.description: On 1 October 1940 Albert Einstein took the oath of allegiance and became a naturalised citizen of the United States, while retaining his Swiss citizenship. The ceremony, conducted by Judge Phillip Forman in New Jersey, formalised the relocation he had effectively made in 1933 when he joined the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. During the war years he lived and worked in Princeton, supporting the Allied cause while continuing his research in unified field theory and engaging in public debates about civil liberties and the responsibilities of scientists. His new citizenship also gave him a permanent base from which to advocate for international control of nuclear energy after 1945.

images.caption: Albert Einstein receiving his certificate of American citizenship from Judge Phillip Forman in New Jersey, 1 October 1940.

events.date_note: In November 1952, after the death of Chaim Weizmann, the Israeli government informally offered Einstein the largely ceremonial post of President of Israel; he declined
events.title: Declines offer to become President of Israel
events.description: In November 1952, following the death of Chaim Weizmann, the government of Israel invited Albert Einstein to become the country’s second president, a largely ceremonial office. Deeply moved but aware of his lack of political and administrative experience, Einstein declined the offer in a letter to Israeli ambassador Abba Eban, explaining that he felt unsuited to dealing with people and official duties. From Princeton he continued to support Zionist and Israeli cultural institutions and to speak out on global issues, advocating for civil rights, nuclear disarmament, and forms of world government while devoting his scientific efforts to an ultimately unsuccessful search for a unified field theory.

events.title: Death in Princeton
events.description: On 18 April 1955 Albert Einstein died at Princeton Hospital in New Jersey at the age of 76, following an abdominal aortic aneurysm. He had refused surgical intervention, stating that he wanted to go when he wished and that prolonging life artificially was tasteless. His body was cremated and his ashes scattered at an undisclosed location, in accordance with his desire to avoid a cult of personality. In his final days he continued to work on equations related to a unified field theory, leaving behind both unfinished calculations and a legacy that permanently reshaped physics and the broader intellectual landscape of the twentieth century.
